title: Brass band instrumentation and the missing E flat clarinets
summary: Clark describes the proper brass band set-up of E flat clarinet, alto, baritone, trombones, cornets and drums. Few young players take up baritone or E flat clarinet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: We can find it. We'll look at a map. What is the difference between those brass bands of that day and the ones of today?

Well, I'll tell you. The difference is now, you see, the brass bands of the day, they don't have the instrumentation like the old brass bands. You see, just like our band. We try to get up to it, but we can't. Because nobody, the young fella, don't want to play the baritone. He don't want to play the alto, which we call the peck horn. And he don't want to play the E flat clarinet. When you have the E flat clarinet, the alto, and the baritone, two trombones, the bass, cornet, three cornets, snad bass drum, you have the real, set up for a brass band. But the fellas up today don't want to play the baritone horn and why, I don't know. Sometimes I wish that I had taken baritone.
How many E flat clarinets are there in town now?

Two to my knowings. Who is that? That's Alphonse Pico and John Cashman. There's the only two E flat players that I know of. There may be some more in the union, these youngsters coming along, you know. But I noticed these school bands, I don't see any E flats. I see a lot of B flats. You see twenty or thirty B flats but you don't see no E. The fellas, I don't know, they're afraid of that instrument like they are the oboe. I hear those fellas, those oboe players, they say that the oboe jar is your head. I don't know why. But the mouthpiece look like a cigar holder.
It's different. Yeah it's different. Did they have many oboe players when you were young?
Oh quite a few. Quite a few. I didn't know them but I remember seeing them. Quite a few.
